items.explanation: The compromise admitted California as a free state and ended the D.C. slave trade, but its tougher Fugitive Slave Act — requiring Northerners to aid in recapturing escapees — outraged the North.
options: A. The strengthened Fugitive Slave Act
B. The ban on slave trading in Washington, D.C.
C. Popular sovereignty in New Mexico territory
D. California's admission as a free state
items.stem: Northerners accepted all parts of the Compromise of 1850 EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the exception. The strengthened Fugitive Slave Act required Northerners to help capture escaped slaves, and it outraged the North; Northerners accepted the rest of the compromise but not this part.
option_explanations.B: Northerners accepted this: the compromise banned the slave trade (though not slavery itself) in Washington, D.C. — a genuine, if limited, antislavery gain.
option_explanations.C: Northerners accepted this: popular sovereignty would decide slavery's fate in the New Mexico and Utah territories, which Northerners expected to remain free.
option_explanations.D: Northerners accepted this: California's admission as a free state was the North's great prize in the compromise.

items.explanation: The Democrats split into Northern and Southern wings, Lincoln won with almost no Southern votes, and slavery in the territories dominated debate — all three statements are true.
options: A. The Democrats split and ran two candidates
B. The winner drew almost no Southern votes
C. Slavery in the territories was a central issue
D. All of the above

option_explanations.A: This is true: the Democrats split into Northern (Douglas) and Southern (Breckinridge) wings and ran two candidates, fatally dividing the party.
option_explanations.B: This is true: Lincoln won the presidency with almost no Southern votes — he was not even on the ballot in most Southern states.
option_explanations.C: This is true: slavery in the territories — whether it could expand westward — was the central issue of the campaign.
option_explanations.D: Correct. All three statements are true: the Democrats split and ran two candidates, Lincoln won with almost no Southern votes, and slavery in the territories dominated the debate.

items.explanation: As coined by journalist John O'Sullivan, Manifest Destiny held that Americans were destined — by Providence — to spread across the continent, a belief mixing economic, political, and racial motives.
options: A. Economics alone drove westward expansion
B. Politics alone drove westward expansion
C. Expansion fulfilled America's providential destiny
D. Eastern overpopulation forced expansion
items.stem: According to the idea of Manifest Destiny,

option_explanations.A: Economics alone did not drive the idea. Manifest Destiny mixed economic, political, and racial motives under a single providential belief — economics was only one strand.
option_explanations.B: Politics alone did not drive the idea. Party politics mattered, but the doctrine itself was a belief about America's destined mission, not mere political maneuvering.
option_explanations.C: Correct. As coined by journalist John O'Sullivan, Manifest Destiny held that Americans were destined by Providence to spread across the continent — expansion as fulfillment of a divine mission.
option_explanations.D: Eastern overpopulation did not force expansion. The East was not overcrowded; expansion was driven by the belief in a providential mission, not by demographic pressure.

items.explanation: Mexico offered enormous land grants to settlers who became Mexican citizens and Catholics — cheap land, not revenge or loyalty to Crockett and Bowie, drew the first Anglo colonists.
options: A. To avenge the Alamo
B. From disillusionment with U.S. Indian policy
C. Out of loyalty to Crockett or Bowie
D. Because Mexico offered vast tracts nearly free
items.stem: American settlers first entered Mexican Texas in the 1820s

option_explanations.A: The Alamo fell in 1836, after Anglo settlement was already well underway. No one settled Texas in the early 1830s to avenge a battle that had not yet happened.
option_explanations.B: Settlers did not come because of U.S. Indian policy. They came for land — Mexico's empresario grants offered enormous tracts nearly free.
option_explanations.C: Crockett and Bowie arrived in Texas in the mid-1830s and died at the Alamo in 1836; they were not the reason settlers had come years earlier.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Mexico offered vast tracts of land nearly free through empresario grants to settlers who became Mexican citizens and Catholics — cheap land, not revenge or loyalty, drew the first Anglo colonists.

items.explanation: The Know-Nothings (the American Party) surged in the early 1850s on a platform of hostility to immigrants and Catholics, demanding longer naturalization periods.
options: A. Free-Soil Party
B. Democratic Party
C. Know-Nothing Party
D. Whig Party
items.stem: The party of this era that championed nativist policies was the

option_explanations.A: The Free-Soil Party opposed the extension of slavery into the territories; it was not a nativist party, though some nativists later joined the Republicans.
option_explanations.B: The Democrats were not the nativist party — they relied heavily on immigrant votes, especially through urban machines like Tammany Hall.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Know-Nothings (the American Party) surged in the early 1850s on hostility to immigrants and Catholics, demanding longer naturalization periods and restrictions on immigrant voting.
option_explanations.D: The Whigs were divided on nativism and never made it their defining cause; the party that championed nativist policies was the Know-Nothings.

items.explanation: The novel electrified the North: it sold hundreds of thousands of copies, was dramatized on stage everywhere, and made the Fugitive Slave Act personally hateful to readers who had wept over Eliza. Lincoln's famous greeting -- 'the little lady who made this big war' -- captures its political force. It converted few Southerners and did not end abolitionism; it inflamed it.
options: A. it was banned throughout the Northern states
B. it turned Northern public opinion against slavery and the Fugitive Slave Act
C. it persuaded Southern planters to free their slaves
D. it brought the abolitionist movement to an end
items.stem: Uncle Tom's Cabin is historically significant because it
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"The object of these sketches is to awaken sympathy and feeling for the African race, as they exist among us; to show their wrongs and sorrows, under a system so necessarily cruel and unjust as to defeat and do away the good effects of all that can be attempted for them."
—Harriet Beecher Stowe, preface to Uncle Tom's Cabin, 1852 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The novel was not banned in the North. It was a Northern bestseller; it was banned and burned in parts of the South.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The novel electrified the North: it sold hundreds of thousands of copies, was dramatized on stages everywhere, and made the Fugitive Slave Act personally hateful to readers who had wept over Eliza's flight.
option_explanations.C: It persuaded few Southern planters. The South denounced the book as slander and answered it with pro-slavery novels of its own.
option_explanations.D: It did not bring abolitionism to an end. It inflamed the abolitionist cause, giving it its most powerful popular weapon.

items.explanation: Stowe pointedly disclaims 'invidious feeling' toward slaveholders, noting that 'some of the noblest of minds and hearts are often thus involved.' The move is strategic: by blaming the system rather than individuals, she keeps moderate Northern readers from closing the book in defensiveness -- moral suasion aimed at conscience, not a call to arms.
options: A. Win over moderate readers by blaming the institution rather than individuals
B. Praise slaveholders as morally admirable people
C. Argue that slavery was economically efficient
D. Call for a violent revolution against the South

The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"The object of these sketches is to awaken sympathy and feeling for the African race, as they exist among us; to show their wrongs and sorrows, under a system so necessarily cruel and unjust as to defeat and do away the good effects of all that can be attempted for them."
—Harriet Beecher Stowe, preface to Uncle Tom's Cabin, 1852 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Stowe pointedly disclaims 'invidious feeling' toward slaveholders, blaming the system rather than individuals — a strategic move to keep moderate Northern readers from closing the book in defensiveness.
option_explanations.B: Stowe does not praise slaveholders as morally admirable. She excuses them only to the extent of blaming the institution; her target is slavery itself.
option_explanations.C: Stowe makes no argument about slavery's economic efficiency. Her argument is moral: the system is 'cruel and unjust,' whatever its economics.
option_explanations.D: Stowe does not call for violent revolution. Her method is moral suasion — awakening conscience through sympathy — not a call to arms.

items.explanation: Stowe's stated method -- 'to awaken sympathy and feeling' through stories of suffering -- is the method of the slave narrative: Douglass's 1845 Narrative used first-person accounts of cruelty to convert readers to abolition. Minstrel shows also depicted Black life, but as racist caricature for entertainment -- the opposite of Stowe's purpose.
options: A. Phrenology textbooks classifying human skulls
B. Railroad timetables coordinating travel
C. Minstrel shows caricaturing Black life for entertainment
D. Abolitionist slave narratives such as Frederick Douglass's Narrative

option_explanations.A: Phrenology textbooks classified skulls to rank races — pseudoscientific racism, the opposite of Stowe's purpose of awakening sympathy.
option_explanations.B: Railroad timetables coordinated travel; they have nothing to do with Stowe's method of moving readers through stories of suffering.
option_explanations.C: Minstrel shows also depicted Black life, but as racist caricature for entertainment — the opposite of Stowe's purpose, which was to make readers feel the cruelty of slavery.
